[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, can you hear me ok?
[00:03] Alex: yep good to go, thanks for setting this up.
[00:06] Maya: cool, quick agenda — we're here to understand your production needs for dedicated capacity, isolation, burst and scaling, and any compliance constraints, then share how Redwood Dedicated can fit. Ethan will jump in on perf details.
[00:18] Priya: quick note on time zones, we've got folks in NY and London so thanks for doing an afternoon slot.
[00:23] Ethan: awesome, I'll keep the deep infra stuff clear then. Alex, can you start with what you're running today?
[00:30] Alex: sure. So currently we run a mix of on-prem inference for some latency sensitive features and cloud endpoints for batch scoring. We use a homegrown routing layer + Kubernetes. Models are a mix of open and proprietary fine-tuned LLMs — mostly 7B to 13B families for retrieval-augmented generation and some reranking tasks. Peak is tricky — daily spikes around market open and close, plus weekly batch runs. We're exploring moving heavy inference to reserved GPUs to get predictable latency and cost.
[01:02] Maya: when you say peak, what's the QPS and token mix?
[01:06] Alex: avg steady-state 40-60 rps on the chat endpoints, but bursts to 300-400 rps for 30-90 seconds during market events; token lengths vary — often 120-400 tokens per request for chat, shorter for rerank.
[01:22] Samir: and critical for us is tail latency — 95th percentile needs to stay under 350ms for our front-end. If it spikes it disrupts traders' workflows.
[01:32] Ethan: useful. Two flavors of offering: hosted (shared) and Dedicated — Dedicated gives isolated GPU pools, reserved capacity, and predictability. For your burst pattern we generally recommend a dedicated pool sized for steady-state with configured burst capacity or pre-warmed spare nodes. We also have autoscale policies that can spin up extra instances but note cold-starts for large models can add seconds.
[02:05] Priya: how does Redwood handle isolation? We need strict tenant isolation and audited logs, plus KMS integration — we can't have any co-tenant GPU sharing.
[02:15] Maya: Dedicated is designed for that — isolated node pools per tenant, customer data plane isolation, and optional VPC/private deployment for on-prem network controls. We also support KMS integrations and audit logging. We'll send SOC2 and our security whitepaper.
[02:33] Alex: good. For scaling, we want autoscale that doesn't break the SLAs. Is there a way to maintain low tail latency during sudden bursts without overprovisioning 24/7?
[02:44] Ethan: yes — the common pattern is a baseline pool sized for normal traffic + a small reserved burst pool kept warm or a rapid-burst lane that can serve lower-latency requests using lighter quantized variants of models. Redwood supports model variants so during capacity constraints you can fallback to a quantized/trimmed variant to preserve latency. Another approach is prefix/KV cache to reduce token work for repeated contexts.
[03:11] Samir: fallbacks sound risky — we need quality to stay high for trader-facing responses. How much degradation when switching to quantized variants?
[03:20] Ethan: depends on model and quant level. For many workflows 4-bit quant can be nearly identical for short prompts; for long-context or high-precision tasks we recommend canary testing. Redwood Optimize can run evals and alert on regressions so you know quality impact.
[03:40] Priya: networking question — if we go Dedicated on Redwood Hosted, how does traffic route? We have strict ingress egress policies and must avoid internet egress for requests with PII.
[03:50] Maya: you can choose Dedicated with VPC peering or a private endpoint so traffic never hits public internet. For stricter controls we offer Private deployment (customer-managed control plane) — that would be the on-prem or VPC-hosted option.
[04:05] Alex: does the Dedicated product guarantee a certain number of GPUs or throughput? We need to lock capacity for critical windows.
[04:12] Maya: Dedicated is reserved capacity — contracts specify committed GPU counts and throughput targets. We also define burst allowances and SLAs for uptime/latency depending on tier. We'll include the contract language in the pricing doc.
[04:25] Samir: pricing — are we billed for max reserved or consumed tokens during bursts?
[04:30] Maya: reserved capacity is a monthly/annual commitment (per GPU-hour or vGPU unit). For bursts beyond committed capacity we have paid burst policies (metered), and options for burst credit pools. We can show modeled cost examples for your workload if you share traces.
[04:50] Alex: we can provide traces. We'll want a cost projection vs our current on-prem spend.
[04:55] Ethan: please do — we'll run a quick cost simulation and recommended instance sizing. Also, if you plan to use mixed model variants, that affects throughput and cost.
[05:08] Priya: another important piece is cold-starts. If autoscale triggers new instances, how long until a model is ready to serve at low latency?
[05:15] Ethan: typical cold-starts depend on model size and infra. For 13B models with optimized kernels and pre-warmed images, we can get under 20s to warm a new instance; larger sizes take longer. For sub-second tail SLAs we recommend keeping a small warm pool or using warm standby instances.
[05:33] Alex: can we pre-load certain hot models at market open and then scale down?
[05:36] Ethan: yes, scheduling scale policies around your market open/close windows is common. You can also use scheduled pre-warms.
[05:42] Samir: compliance — we need SOC2, proof of encryption at rest and in transit, and KMS integration; also audit logs for model access.
[05:51] Maya: noted — Redwood supports TLS in transit, envelope encryption via KMS, and provides audit logs. We'll attach SOC2 report and a short security summary. For extremely sensitive workloads we recommend Private deployment.
[06:03] Priya: ok. One more: model rollouts — we do iterative rollouts and need canary and A/B experiments across model versions. Does Redwood support that?
[06:11] Ethan: yes — rollouts, canaries, A/B testing, automatic fallback policies are supported in the Console. You can pin model versions per route.
[06:20] Alex: for the pilot we'd like Redwood to run a benchmark against our traces to validate latency and cost. Could that be done on Dedicated?
[06:27] Ethan: absolutely — we typically run a two-stage pilot: first lab benchmarks on workload traces to size instances and estimate cost, then a short production pilot with traffic mirroring. We can do the lab bench in a week if traces are available.
[06:39] Samir: timeline wise — we want to evaluate options this quarter and have a pilot in early December. Is that feasible?
[06:45] Maya: yes — we can send pricing and security docs this week and schedule the pilot week of Dec 14 as suggested.
[06:52] Alex: ok good. A few technical nitpicks: we have an internal auth flow with SSO (SAML), RBAC expectations, and we'd like per-route cost breakdowns for chargeback.
[07:02] Maya: Redwood Console has token-level cost breakdowns and per-route dashboards; we also integrate with SSO/SAML and RBAC controls.
[07:10] Priya: curious about hardware options — do you support multiple GPU types and can we choose A100 vs H100 or the equivalent?
[07:17] Ethan: yes — Dedicated offers GPU family options; kernel and compilation selection is hardware-aware. We can recommend H100-like instances for throughput-heavy models. We'll include recommended instance types for your workload.
[07:29] Alex: another practical question — who runs the control plane for Dedicated? Is it Redwood-managed or customer-managed?
[07:34] Maya: by default the control plane is Redwood-managed for hosted Dedicated; you get isolated data plane. For Private deployments the control plane can be customer-managed in your VPC or on-prem. That option is typical for regulated banks.
[07:46] Samir: ok that helps. Any vendor lock-in concerns with model format or runtime? We want to keep portability.
[07:52] Ethan: Redwood supports common ONNX/transformer formats and we aim for model portability; we also document execution specifics. We can provide a migration path if you ever want to move.
[08:02] [Short pause — background noise]
[08:10] Alex: one more — monitoring and alerts. We need detailed tracing and error analysis for production.
[08:15] Ethan: Console provides tracing hooks, per-route metrics, token-level latency breakdowns and error analysis. We can hook into your observability stack.
[08:24] Priya: good. Let's talk procurement: we'll need contract terms for annual reserved capacity with SLAs. Can you share standard terms?
[08:31] Maya: yes, we'll include standard enterprise T&Cs and SLA language. Pricing sheet will include monthly and annual commit options.

[08:41] Maya: we can schedule a short Console walkthrough as part of the pilot kickoff.
